questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An exposed frame on a tall elevation
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an exposed frame is described as honest construction
questions.stem: Explain why a tall building with an exposed frame is often described as honest in its construction.

answer.exemplar: An exposed frame shows the structure doing its work. The columns, the beams between them and the diagonal braces can all be read from outside, so a viewer can see how the weight of the building is carried down to the foundations, and the panels of wall fill in the frame rather than pretending to be structure. The result is a building whose appearance is explained by its construction, which is what the word honest is being asked to mean.

questions.explanation: An exposed frame lets the viewer read the load path from the roof down through the columns to the ground, and the wall panels are openly infill. The building's appearance is therefore explained by its structure.
questions.hint: Ask what the viewer can see and follow.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how an interior designer can slow a visitor down
questions.stem: Explain how an interior designer can make a visitor move more slowly through a room.

answer.exemplar: Movement is slowed by making the straight way ahead hard to follow and the interesting way easy. A stair that curves, a niche that interrupts a wall, or a doorway set off the axis all delay the visitor without blocking the route, and each pause is a chance to look at something. Where the ceiling painting, the pavement pattern and the axis of the windows are all pulled out of true, the eye is carried sideways and the body follows more slowly than a straight corridor would allow.

questions.explanation: Curving stairs, off-axis doorways and misaligned ceilings interrupt the straight route and pull the eye sideways, so the visitor pauses. A straight corridor with a clear view hurries them through.
questions.hint: Interrupt the straight line of travel.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a villa plan separates visitors from the work of the household
questions.stem: Explain how a Palladian villa plan arranges the movement of people and goods.

answer.exemplar: The plan separates the public and the service halves of the house without splitting it in two. The main entrance, the portico and the central hall lie on the axis, and the rooms of the household are arranged symmetrically about it, while a wing set at right angles on one side carries the kitchen, stores and servants' access, reaching the outside world by its own route. A visitor therefore comes to the front and is drawn inwards, and the work of the household circulates behind and to one side.

questions.explanation: The portico and central hall draw the visitor along the axis, while a service wing set at right angles carries the household's work on its own route. The two circulations never have to share a door.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why an arch outlives a lintel
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an arch spans further than a lintel of the same stone
questions.stem: Explain why an arch can span a wider opening than a lintel of the same material and thickness.

answer.exemplar: A lintel carries its load by bending, so it needs to be deep in proportion to the span, and stone in tension cracks, which limits how far a single stone can reach. An arch carries the same load by compression, squeezing wedge-shaped blocks against one another, so a shallow ring of voussoirs can span much further and can be built up in small units. The arch also delivers its thrust into the abutments instead of needing a deep beam of stone underneath.

questions.explanation: A lintel must be deep in proportion to its span because it bends, and stone cracks in tension. An arch spans by compression in shallow wedges, so it reaches much further with far less material.
questions.hint: Ask how each form carries its load.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a dressed stone lintel cannot span far
questions.stem: Explain why a lintel of dressed stone is limited in the width of opening it can span.

answer.exemplar: A lintel is a beam, and a beam resists load by bending, which puts the underside of the stone in tension. Dressed stone is excellent in compression and very poor in tension, so as the span grows the tension at the underside rises faster than the section can resist, and the stone cracks. The limit is therefore set by the depth of the lintel, and the depth needed rises almost in proportion to the span, so the opening cannot be widened without a much deeper beam.

questions.explanation: A lintel resists by bending, which puts tension in the underside where dressed stone is weak, so the deeper the beam the more it can carry. A wider opening needs a much deeper lintel or it cracks.
questions.hint: Think about the underside of the stone.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why Romanesque windows are small and set high
questions.stem: Explain why a Romanesque church has small windows set high in the nave wall.

answer.exemplar: The windows are small and high because the wall is not there for light, it is there for strength. A heavy barrel or groin vault pushes outwards at its springing, and the wall's job is to resist that push, so the thickness of the wall cannot be reduced to make room for a large opening. The builders therefore kept the windows narrow, pushed them up above the aisle roofs where the wall was no longer needed to brace, and accepted dim interiors lit by the small openings.

questions.explanation: The wall's mass resists the thrust of the heavy vault, so it cannot be thinned to take a large window. Small openings set high, where the wall is free of the vault's push, keep the structure sound.
questions.hint: The wall is doing structural work.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the logic of a heavy base, tall middle and light top
questions.stem: Explain why a palace front was designed with a heavy base, a tall middle and a light top.

answer.exemplar: The three parts answer three different needs at once. The heavy base carries the weight of the building and gives the entrance a solid, protected base, with rustication making that mass visible. The tall middle holds the principal rooms, which need tall windows and high ceilings to be worthy of the household, and it is given the richest order to mark that importance. The light attic above crowns the composition, hides the roof and keeps the front from ending in a heavy mass.

questions.explanation: The base carries the weight and looks solid, the middle holds the principal rooms in the richest order, and the attic crowns the front lightly. Each part answers a different need of the hierarchy.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An exposed frame on a tall elevation
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a metal frame allowed large windows and thin walls
questions.stem: Explain how a tall building with a metal frame was able to have large windows and thin walls.

answer.exemplar: A load-bearing wall must be deep enough to carry the weight of what stands above it and to resist the pushes of the vaults and roof, and a wall of that kind can only be pierced by small openings. Once the loads are carried down slender columns of iron or steel, the wall is left with no structural duty and can be reduced to a thin skin, which can be opened up with large areas of glass. The frame therefore sets the wall free, and the window size stops being limited by the wall's strength.

questions.explanation: A load-bearing wall can only take small openings, but a frame carries the loads instead, leaving the wall as a thin skin that can be largely glazed. The frame sets the window size free.
questions.hint: Ask what the wall no longer has to carry.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a villa is set at the end of an open approach
questions.stem: Explain why a Palladian villa is often set at the end of an approach across a lawn.

answer.exemplar: The approach is part of the composition, not simply the way the house is reached. A long axis across open ground lets the visitor see the whole front of the villa at once, with the portico and the balanced wings presented as a single picture, and the building appears larger and more symmetrical than it would from a crowded street. The empty ground also lets the small temple or grotto at the far end of the axis be seen as the terminal point of the view.

questions.explanation: A long open approach lets the visitor read the whole symmetrical front as one picture and lets the axis end in a focal point. The front is designed to be seen from a distance.
questions.hint: Think about what the visitor sees on the way.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Count the doorways joining a straight enfilade of rooms
questions.stem: A clerk's file note records a suite of eight rooms whose doorways are all set on one axis, so that the visitor sees straight through the suite. How many doorways join those eight rooms in a single line?
questions.explanation: Eight rooms in a single line are joined by seven doorways, because each room after the first needs one opening to the next. The same count gives the number of views the eye travels through.
questions.hint: One fewer doorway than rooms.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An exposed frame on a tall elevation
questions.learningObjective: Read columns rising above the top floor of a framed building

stimulus.body: A clerk's file note describes a tall building whose exposed steel columns rise above the top floor and carry a heavy cornice, while the wall panels stop below them. The note asks what the exposed columns tell a reader.

questions.stem: According to the file note, what do the exposed columns above the top floor tell a reader?

options.text: That the columns are decorative and were added to give the top a richer look
options.misconception: calls the exposed columns purely decorative

options.text: That the building's extra storeys are a later addition above the original cornice
options.misconception: reads the continued frame as a later extension

options.text: That the frame continues to the very top and carries the cornice, not the wall
That the panels are thinner at the top than they are lower down
options.misconception: claims the panel thickness changes with height

questions.explanation: Columns that run past the top floor and carry the cornice show the frame goes all the way up, so the heaviest element at the parapet is carried by the structure below. The wall stops short because it carries nothing.
questions.hint: Ask what the cornice is resting on.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Name the crowning moulding of a classical palace front
questions.stem: First: name the heavy projecting moulding that runs along the top of a classical palace front. Second: what does it do for the front?

options.text: The architrave, and it crowns and closes the whole composition of the front
options.misconception: names the band over the columns as the crowning member

options.text: The plinth, and it crowns and closes the whole composition of the front
options.misconception: names the base moulding as the crowning member

options.text: The string course, and it crowns and closes the whole composition of the front
options.misconception: names a mid-wall band as the crowning member

options.text: The cornice, and it crowns and closes the whole composition of the front

questions.explanation: The first step names the cornice, and the second asks what it does: as the heaviest and most projecting member at the top, it gathers the storeys into one crowned composition and hides the roof behind it.
questions.hint: It is the topmost projecting band.
